12327.heading: Fixed-Point Iteration
12327.content:
Fixed-point iteration begins with $x_0$ and repeatedly computes $x_{k+1}=g(x_k)$. If the sequence converges, its limit satisfies $g(p)=p$ and is a [[Fixed Point]].

A sufficient local condition is that $g$ maps an interval into itself and has derivative magnitude below one there. A poor rearrangement can make the same equation diverge.

12330.title: Fixed Point
12330.heading: Fixed Point
12330.content:
A fixed point of a function $g$ is a value $p$ satisfying $g(p)=p$. An equation $f(x)=0$ can often be rearranged into an equivalent fixed-point equation.

The rearrangement matters because different choices of $g$ can have different convergence behavior. [[Fixed-Point Iteration]] succeeds locally when the mapping contracts distances around the fixed point.

12333.title: Fixed Field
12333.heading: Fixed Field
12333.content:
The fixed field of a group of field automorphisms consists of elements left unchanged by every automorphism in the group. It is a subfield of the extension.

The Galois correspondence pairs subgroups with fixed fields in reverse inclusion order.

12345.title: Fitts's Law
12345.heading: Fitts's Law
12345.content:
Fitts's law models the time required to make an aimed movement to a target:

$$
MT = a + b\log_2(2D/W)
$$

$MT$ is movement time, $D$ is distance to the target, $W$ is target width, and $a$ and $b$ are fitted constants. Movement takes longer as distance increases or the target becomes narrower.

The logarithmic term is the index of difficulty. Dividing that index by movement time gives an index of performance in bits per second, which can compare [[Input Device]]s. The law captures an important speed-accuracy relationship in [[Motor Control]] and [[Object Selection]].

12354.title: Fisher Exact Test
12354.heading: Fisher Exact Test
12354.content:
Fisher's exact test evaluates association in a contingency table by calculating probabilities under fixed marginal totals. It does not rely on the large-sample chi-squared approximation and is therefore useful when cells are small.

The test provides evidence about dependence between the categorical variables, not the size or practical importance of the association. Frequencies and proportions should still accompany its p-value.

The source motivates the method through Fisher's tea-tasting experiment: under random guessing and fixed margins, the probability of each table follows from the possible label arrangements. This makes the test an exact association procedure rather than a normal or t approximation.

12375.title: First Isomorphism Theorem for Rings
12375.heading: First Isomorphism Theorem for Rings
12375.content:
For a [[Ring Homomorphism]] f: R → S, the image of f is isomorphic to the [[Quotient Ring]] R/ker(f). Elements of R that differ by an element of the kernel have the same image, and no further identifications occur.

The theorem converts a mapping problem into an ideal-and-quotient problem. In particular, every surjective ring homomorphism presents its target as the source divided by its kernel.

The text presents this as the ring analogue of the group theorem, often abbreviated FHT. When the homomorphism is onto, the target is isomorphic to the source divided by the exact ideal of elements sent to zero.

12387.title: Firewall
12387.heading: Firewall
12387.content:
A firewall is a logical or physical boundary that allows or blocks network traffic according to defined rules. It can protect the edge of a cloud environment and separate internal security containers so only traffic appropriate to a service can cross.

Rules can restrict ports, protocols, sources, and destinations, while logs record rejected or accepted activity for monitoring. A firewall is one layer of defense and does not replace application authorization, endpoint protection, or secure data handling.

Within [[Defense in Depth]], a firewall regulates incoming and outgoing traffic at a network boundary according to a defined security policy. It can prevent an attack from moving freely between public and private networks, but it cannot repair a trusted user who executes a malicious payload.

12399.title: Finite Precision and Error Accumulation
12399.heading: Finite Precision and Error Accumulation
12399.content:
Digital machines represent numbers with a finite number of bits, so many values must be rounded. In a long numerical calculation, small representation and round-off errors can accumulate until the result is no longer trustworthy.

Numerical methods control this risk through stable formulations, bounded errors, and checks on intermediate results. More hardware speed does not repair an unstable method; it can merely produce the wrong answer faster.

12408.content:
The finite element method replaces a continuous thermal domain with a collection of small elements joined at nodes. Within each element, temperature is approximated from nodal values, allowing the governing heat equation to become a finite system of algebraic equations.

Discretization makes irregular geometry and nonuniform properties tractable, but it introduces approximation error. Finite element electromagnetic analysis subdivides an electromagnetic domain into elements, approximates a potential or field inside each element, assembles local equations, applies interface and external boundary conditions, and solves the resulting system.

Finite element discretization divides a physical domain into elements and nodes. The analyst chooses element type, size, and arrangement so the mesh can approximate the geometry and expected field variation.

Discretization converts an infinite-dimensional continuum problem into finitely many nodal unknowns. Finer or higher-order elements can improve accuracy, but they also increase the size and cost of the assembled equations.

Finite element assembly combines local element equations into one global system for the complete domain. Each local row and column is placed according to the global numbers of its associated nodal degrees of freedom.

Contributions from elements meeting at a node are added, which expresses equilibrium and compatibility across the mesh. The resulting matrix is typically sparse because an element couples only degrees of freedom in its local neighborhood.

Finite element analysis is a numerical procedure that replaces a continuous engineering domain with a finite collection of simpler elements connected at nodes. An assumed response inside each element relates nodal unknowns to loads or other inputs.

Element equations are assembled into a global system, modified by boundary conditions, and solved for primary field variables. Secondary quantities such as stress, strain, heat flux, or velocity are then recovered from that nodal solution.

12441.heading: Filtering
12441.content:
Filtering estimates the present hidden state from observations available through the present time. A recursive filter alternates prediction through the transition model with correction through the observation model.

The operation answers the time-indexed question with no offset between the searched state and the latest evidence. It differs from prediction of future states and smoothing of past states.

12444.heading: Filtered Ring
12444.content:
A filtered ring has a descending sequence R = R₀ ⊇ R₁ ⊇ R₂ ⊇ ··· such that RₘRₙ is contained in Rₘ₊ₙ. The index records increasing order or depth in the filtration.

Passing to successive quotients Rₙ/Rₙ₊₁ produces the [[Associated Graded Ring]]. Powers of an ideal give the important [[I-Adic Filtration]].

12447.sourceSearchName: filter feature selection model filter feature selection model
12447.title: Filter Feature Selection Model
12447.heading: Filter Feature Selection Model
12447.content:
A filter feature selection model scores variables from general properties of the training data before a particular classifier is fitted. Common criteria measure correlation, information, dependency, consistency, or distance between classes.

Separating selection from classifier training makes filters comparatively efficient and reduces interaction between the selector's bias and the learner's bias. The tradeoff is that a high-scoring subset may not be optimal for the eventual classification algorithm.

Within a broader taxonomy, filters contrast with wrappers, hybrids, and embedded methods. Their model independence makes them reusable and scalable, although their scoring assumptions determine which dependencies they can recognize.

For high-dimensional Big Data, filters are attractive because they avoid fitting a classifier for every candidate subset. Distributed scoring can extend that advantage, although pairwise relevance and redundancy measures may still be expensive.

12450.title: Filter Bank
12450.heading: Filter Bank
12450.content:
A filter bank divides the frequency spectrum of a speech frame into bands and measures the energy in each band. These measurements approximate the distribution of acoustic energy that distinguishes speech sounds.

The band energies form part of a [[Feature Vector]]. Applying the same bank across successive [[Speech Frame|frames]] produces a time-varying representation for an [[Acoustic Model]].

12483.title: Field
12483.heading: Field
12483.content:
A field is a nonzero [[Commutative Ring]] in which every nonzero element has a [[Multiplicative Inverse]]. Its only ideals are the zero ideal and the whole ring.

Every field is an [[Integral Domain]]. Conversely, a quotient by a [[Maximal Ideal]] is a field, so maximal ideals mark the places where a ring can be reduced to field-valued arithmetic.

The book moves from fields as special domains to fields as coefficient systems for polynomial division and as the base and extension objects of Galois theory. Finite domains and maximal-ideal quotients provide two important constructions of fields.

12489.title: Field of View
12489.heading: Field of View
12489.content:
Field of view is the maximum visual angle that can be seen instantaneously on a display. It is measured in degrees and can vary with the user's position and orientation relative to the screen.

Field of view describes what is visible at one moment, while [[Field of Regard]] describes the larger surrounding region in which imagery can be displayed. A tracked [[Head-Worn Display]] may have a modest field of view but a 360-degree field of regard because the display moves with the head.

A wider field of view can support peripheral vision, visual search, and spatial awareness, but it is only one component of [[Display Fidelity]].

AR often has a narrower augmented field than the user's unobstructed physical view. Virtual content can therefore disappear at an artificial image boundary even though its real referent remains visible, making off-screen cues and deliberate content placement important.

In a perspective game camera, field of view is an input to the projection matrix. An excessively narrow value magnifies camera motion and can hide surrounding context, while a very wide value increases peripheral coverage but distorts the image near its edges.

12492.title: Field Automorphism
12492.heading: Field Automorphism

Composition and inverse make the relevant automorphisms into a group.

12495.content:
Field of regard is the amount of physical space around a user in which a [[Visual Display]] can present imagery. It is measured in degrees of visual angle.

It differs from [[Field of View]], which is the portion visible at a single instant. A cylindrical display may offer a 360-degree horizontal field of regard. A tracked [[Head-Worn Display]] can also provide a 360-degree field of regard because the display remains in front of the eyes as the user turns, even when its instantaneous field of view is much smaller.

Field of regard is one component of [[Display Fidelity]].

12504.heading: Feedforward Neural Computation
12504.content:
Feedforward neural computation passes input values through weighted sums and activation functions from the input layer toward the output layer without sending values backward during prediction.

Each layer's output becomes the next layer's input. During training, a separate backward pass uses the resulting error to calculate weight updates.

Kelleher represents a dense feedforward network as a chain of [[Layer Matrix Computation|matrix multiplications]] with elementwise nonlinear activations between them. This expresses the same computations as a diagram of connected neurons but makes the repeated weighted-sum work more suitable for matrix-oriented hardware.

12507.title: Feedback
12507.heading: Feedback
12507.content:
Feedback is information that helps a user understand system state, the result of an operation, or progress on a task. It can come from the system, the environment, or the user's own body.

Sensory feedback may be visual, auditory, haptic, chemical, proprioceptive, or kinesthetic. Reactive feedback comes from operating the interface, instrumental feedback comes from controls and tools, and operational feedback communicates the system's result.

Useful feedback closes the [[User-System Loop]] and supports an accurate [[Conceptual Model]]. Multiple channels can reinforce one another, but they should maintain [[Feedback Compliance]] in space and time.

In a [[Game-Player System]], feedback is also the return path by which the result of a player's action changes the [[Player Mental Model]]. A behavior should provide timely, comprehensible evidence of relevant state change; missing or inexplicable feedback prevents the player from testing predictions and weakens [[Engagement]].

A [[Robust Game Verb]] provides feedback even when an action is refused. A sound, animation, or other visible reaction can teach why an object resists the verb instead of leaving the player uncertain whether the input was received.

12510.title: Fermi Energy
12510.heading: Fermi Energy
12510.content: Fermi energy is the highest occupied energy of a solid's free electrons at absolute zero. These electrons do not behave like an ordinary classical gas: only a limited number can occupy each quantum state. At a higher temperature, some electrons near the Fermi level enter higher available states. This energy distribution helps explain electronic transport and [[Thermionic Emission]].

12513.title: Fetch API
12513.heading: Fetch API
12513.content:
The Fetch API is a browser interface for making asynchronous network requests with a promise-based programming model. It offers a more direct and readable alternative to using raw [[XMLHttpRequest]] callbacks.

Angular applications normally use [[Angular HttpClient]] because it integrates with dependency injection, typed responses, interceptors, and observables. Fetch remains a browser-level alternative rather than an Angular-specific service.

12516.title: Feedback Versus Input
12516.heading: Feedback Versus Input
12516.content:
Playtest feedback describes where the game did or did not produce the intended experience. Input proposes a change to the work. Both can be useful, but they carry different authority.

The designer owns the diagnosis and solution because a tester's suggestion may solve a different problem or contradict the project's values. Separating the observed shortfall from the proposed feature lets the team consider several remedies without dismissing the underlying evidence.

12519.title: Feedback Loop
12519.heading: Feedback Loop
12519.content:
A feedback loop exists when changes produced by interacting parts return to influence the conditions that produced them. This circular causality turns a connected process into a [[Complex System]].

The two broad forms are the [[Reinforcing Loop]], which magnifies a direction of change, and the [[Balancing Loop]], which counteracts deviation. Complex behavior commonly arises from several such loops operating together at different levels and timescales.

A live product creates an operational loop when a team plans a change, develops and deploys it, measures player response, and uses that evidence to decide what follows. The value of speed lies in shortening the complete learning cycle rather than implementation alone.

12522.title: Feedback Compliance
12522.heading: Feedback Compliance
12522.content:
Feedback compliance is the spatial and temporal agreement among the forms of [[Feedback]] a user receives.

Directional compliance means a virtual object moves in the same direction as the physical control. Nulling compliance means returning a device to its initial pose also returns the controlled object to its corresponding pose. Temporal compliance means feedback arrives without a disruptive delay; [[Latency]] is a common violation.

When visual information conflicts with proprioceptive, kinesthetic, vestibular, or other cues, performance can degrade. Strong conflicts can also produce disorientation and [[Cybersickness]].

12525.title: Federated Security
12525.heading: Federated Security
12525.content: Federated security lets an application rely on a trusted identity provider to authenticate a person or service and issue a token carrying identity claims. Several applications can accept that trusted identity, enabling a shared sign-on experience without each application managing a separate password store. The application must still validate the token and decide which resources the authenticated subject may use; delegated identity does not delegate every authorization decision.

12528.title: Federated Learning
12528.heading: Federated Learning
12528.content:
Federated learning trains a shared model by sending the model to participating devices, updating it on local data, and aggregating model changes rather than collecting the raw examples centrally.

For assistants, this can reduce the amount of private speech or interaction data transferred off a device. It does not eliminate every privacy risk, but it changes the training architecture so personal data can remain local.

The book also describes the architecture for phones and hospitals contributing to a shared project: a local model learns from each site's records, and an aggregator combines updates to improve a central model. Sharing model changes rather than raw records reduces central collection but does not, by itself, settle every disclosure risk.

12531.title: Feature
12531.heading: Feature
12531.content:
A feature is an attribute or variable used to describe an aspect of a data object. Useful features make objects distinguishable, support interpretable models, and provide the measurements on which classification, regression, clustering, retrieval, and other analytic tasks operate.

Feature meaning depends on the application. A color may be categorical, age numerical, and degree ordinal. The value of a feature is therefore inseparable from its domain, measurement scale, and the analytic question it is intended to answer.

12534.title: Feature-Weighted K-Means
12534.heading: Feature-Weighted K-Means
12534.content:
Feature-weighted K-means extends the usual partitioning objective by learning how strongly each dimension contributes to distance. Cluster assignments, centroids, and feature weights are updated so that informative dimensions receive greater influence.

Some variants learn one global weight vector, while others allow each cluster to emphasize a different subspace. Without regularization, weights can collapse onto a few dimensions, so constraints or penalties are used to maintain a useful balance.

12537.title: Feature-Representation Transfer Learning
12537.heading: Feature-Representation Transfer Learning
12537.content:
Feature-representation transfer learning constructs a space in which source knowledge and target observations become more compatible. The transformation may encode shared factors, reduce distribution distance, or combine source-specific and target-specific components.

After alignment, a classifier can use labeled source structure to support a sparsely labeled target. A representation that aligns marginal distributions while mixing class boundaries can create negative transfer, so class relevance remains essential.

Kelleher gives a concrete neural example: early layers of an image-trained [[Convolutional Neural Network]] may already detect low-level visual patterns useful for a related target task. A project can keep those layers, replace later task-specific layers, and train the hybrid model with a smaller labeled dataset. The transfer works best when the source features are relevant; reusing a representation is not a substitute for checking its target-task performance.

12540.title: Feature-Based Forecasting
12540.heading: Feature-Based Forecasting
12540.content:
Feature-based forecasting uses characteristics of a time series to choose, combine, or configure forecasting models. Features describe properties such as trend, seasonality, dependence, entropy, and forecastability.

Instead of assuming one forecaster is best for every series, the feature space relates series behavior to model performance. An instance-space view can also reveal regions where current forecasting methods succeed or leave gaps.

12543.title: Feature Vector
12543.heading: Feature Vector
12543.content:
A feature vector is an ordered set of numerical measurements representing one observation. In speech recognition, it commonly summarizes the spectral properties of a short [[Speech Frame]].

A sequence of feature vectors is more compact and model-ready than the original waveform. The [[Acoustic Model]] uses the sequence to estimate which phonetic states most plausibly produced the signal.

More generally, a feature vector assigns one value to each feature selected for a data object. Using a fixed feature set places heterogeneous objects into a common coordinate representation, allowing learning algorithms to compare, partition, or predict them.
